title: Write a `UnaryOperator<String>` that trims and lowercases a name.
shortTitle: Write a UnaryOperator<String> that trims and lowercases a name

s1_definition.profdef: `UnaryOperator<T>` is a specialisation of `Function<T, T>` where the input and output types are the same. A `UnaryOperator<String>` transforms a String into another String, here trimming whitespace and lowercasing.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya tidies up messy names: she strips the extra spaces and makes everything lowercase so the records are consistent. Same thing in, cleaned-up same thing out.
s1_definition.oneliner: `UnaryOperator<String>` is a `Function<String, String>` — ideal for normalising a string to the same type.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `UnaryOperator<T>` is a specialisation of `Function<T, T>` where the input and output types are the same. A `UnaryOperator<String>` transforms a String into another String, here trimming whitespace and lowercasing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya tidies up messy names: she strips the extra spaces and makes everything lowercase so the records are consistent. Same thing in, cleaned-up same thing out.

**One line to remember:** `UnaryOperator<String>` is a `Function<String, String>` — ideal for normalising a string to the same type.

sections.s2_technical:
UnaryOperator extends Function with both type parameters equal, so `UnaryOperator<String> normalise = s -> s.trim().toLowerCase()` cleans a name. It is used anywhere a same-type transformation is natural, such as `list.replaceAll(normalise)`, which rewrites each element of a list in place.

Because it is a Function, it inherits `andThen` and `compose`, so you can chain normalisation steps, for example `((UnaryOperator<String>) String::trim).andThen(String::toLowerCase)`. Using UnaryOperator rather than Function signals intent — the operation preserves the type — which makes APIs like `List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator)` read clearly.

The senior nuance is choosing `trim` versus `strip`: `strip` is Unicode-aware and introduced in Java 11, so for modern code it is the better default. I also keep normalisation a single, well-named operator so the same canonicalisation is reused everywhere names are compared or stored, avoiding subtle mismatches between code paths. Type-preserving transformations are exactly what UnaryOperator documents.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Names arrive at the National Bank of India with stray spaces and inconsistent casing, causing duplicate-looking records, so every name must be normalised the same way before storage or comparison.

This is exactly what a UnaryOperator does — a single trim-and-lowercase operator canonicalises each name consistently.

The code defines a `NameNormalizer` with the operator and a demo using replaceAll.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a list with "  Rajesh ", "PRIYA", " Amit".

Step 1: replaceAll applies the operator to each element in place.

Step 2: For "  Rajesh ", strip removes the surrounding spaces and toLowerCase gives "rajesh".

Step 3: "PRIYA" becomes "priya" and " Amit" becomes "amit".

Step 4: The list is rewritten in place to the normalised forms.

```
INFO: normalized: [rajesh, priya, amit]
INFO: single    : vikram
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ["  Rajesh ", "PRIYA", " Amit"]
    │ replaceAll(s -> s.strip().toLowerCase())
    ▼
  ["rajesh", "priya", "amit"]   ← same list, rewritten in place
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Name Canonicalisation ═══

  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ──clean names──→ store/compare
  │ raw names│→│ NameNormalizer   │
  │          │ │ strip+lowercase  │
  └──────────┘ └──────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — UnaryOperator<String> ═══

  ┌─ same-type transform ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T> (input == output)   │
  │ s -> s.strip().toLowerCase()                               │
  │ List.replaceAll(UnaryOperator) rewrites in place           │
  │ inherits andThen/compose for chaining steps                │
  │ prefer strip() (Unicode-aware, Java 11+) over trim()       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │          NameNormalizer       │
  │  - normalize: UnaryOperator    │ strip().toLowerCase()
  │  + normalize(String): String   │ apply
  │  + normalizeAll(List): void     │ replaceAll
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. names.replaceAll(normalize)
  2. per element: strip().toLowerCase()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A UnaryOperator is a specialisation of Function where the input and output types are the same, so a UnaryOperator of String is the natural type for normalising a name. I define it as a lambda that strips the whitespace and lowercases the string, and because it is type-preserving I can hand it straight to List dot replaceAll, which rewrites every element of a list in place.

At the National Bank of India names arrived with stray spaces and inconsistent casing, which created duplicate-looking records, so I funnel every name through a single normalise operator before storing or comparing. Using UnaryOperator rather than a plain Function documents the intent that the operation preserves the type, and since it is still a Function I can chain steps with andThen or compose when the canonicalisation grows.

The senior point I add is to prefer strip over trim, because strip is Unicode-aware and is the better default in modern Java, and to keep the normalisation in one well-named operator so the exact same canonicalisation is reused across every code path. That consistency is what prevents subtle mismatches where one path lowercases and another does not, which is a common source of phantom duplicates.
